t.6.48.1: Having entered the city of Laṅkā, tormented by fear of Rāma's arrows, the king, his pride now broken, became shaken in all his senses.
t.6.48.2: Like an elephant overpowered by a lion, like a serpent by Garuḍa, the king was overwhelmed by the great-souled Rāghava.
t.6.48.3: Remembering the arrows of Rāghava, which shone like the rod of Brahmā and blazed with a splendor like lightning, the lord of the rākṣasas trembled with anguish.
t.6.48.4: Having seated himself upon his supreme, divine throne made of gold, Rāvaṇa, looking around at the Rākṣasas, spoke these words.
t.6.48.5: All that supreme austerity which I performed has surely been in vain for me, since I, the equal of the great Indra, have been conquered by a mere human being.
t.6.48.7: I obtained the boon of being unslayable by Devas, Dānavas, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas and Pannagas, but I did not ask for it from men.
t.6.48.6: This is that dreadful utterance of Brahmā which has now come upon me: “Know that your danger comes from humans.” So it has proved to be.
t.6.48.8: Having taken up this very task, you must make every effort here; and let the Rākṣasas also take their stand on the summits of the patrol-ways and the gate-towers.
t.6.48.9: Let Kumbhakarṇa be awakened, he who is of matchless depth and who crushes the pride of the gods and Dānavas, but who lies overpowered by Brahmā's curse.
t.6.48.10: Knowing that he himself had been defeated and that Prahasta had been slain, that mighty one issued orders to the fearsome army of the rākṣasas.
t.6.48.11: Let vigilance be maintained at the gates, and let the ramparts be mounted; let Kumbhakarṇa, who lies overcome by the power of sleep, be awakened.
t.6.48.12: The rākṣasa sleeps for nine, six, seven and eight months at a time; wake him quickly, Kumbhakarṇa of mighty strength!
t.6.48.13: For he, the mighty-armed one, the foremost of all the Rākṣasas, will swiftly slay in battle the Vānaras and the two princes.
t.6.48.14: Kumbhakarṇa, deluded and devoted to vulgar pleasures, lies forever asleep, while for one routed by Rāma this battle has come to a most dreadful pass.
t.6.48.15: Once Kumbhakarṇa is awakened, I shall have no more grief; otherwise, what shall I do with him, though his strength is equal to Śakra's?
t.6.48.17: Commanded by Rāvaṇa, those eaters of flesh and blood, greatly agitated, went to the dwelling of Kumbhakarṇa.
t.6.48.16: Whoever does not come forward to help when such a calamity has befallen... But those rākṣasas, having heard that speech of the lord of the rākṣasas,
t.6.48.18: Taking perfumes and garlands, as well as foods, they went in haste and entered that great-gated abode, which stretched a yojana on every side.
t.6.48.19: Advancing with difficulty, they strenuously made their way into the cave, the lovely cave of Kumbhakarṇa that wafted every kind of fragrance.
t.6.48.20: Having entered that delightful, splendid cave with its floor of gold, they beheld the tiger among the Nairṛtas lying asleep, terrible to behold.
t.6.48.21: But they, all together, set about waking Kumbhakarṇa, sunk in deep slumber, who lay sleeping, grotesque in form, like a mountain scattered in pieces.
t.6.48.23: They saw him, Kumbhakarṇa of mighty strength, that tiger among the Nairṛtas, with his terrible nostrils and his mouth as vast as Pātāla.
t.6.48.22: Him whose body bristled with upright hair, hissing like a serpent, terrifying all with his mighty breaths as he lay sleeping, dreadful to behold.
t.6.48.24: Then those great-souled ones piled up before Kumbhakarṇa a heap of meats like Mount Meru, supremely satisfying.
t.6.48.25: The tigers among the Nairṛtas made heaps of deer, buffaloes and boars, and a wondrous mound of food as well.
t.6.48.27: And they anointed the scorcher of foes with the most precious sandalwood paste, and covered him with heavenly garlands and sweet-smelling fragrances.
t.6.48.26: Then the enemies of the thirty gods placed pots of blood and various kinds of liquor before Kumbhakarṇa.
t.6.48.28: The demons in their thousands released fragrant incense and praised the scorcher of foes, and they roared aloud like thundering rain-clouds.
t.6.48.29: They blew their conches, whose lustre was like that of the moon, and, enraged, they all at once roared a tumultuous roar.
t.6.48.30: Those night-rangers roared, slapped their arms and tossed him about; to awaken Kumbhakarṇa they raised a tremendous din.
t.6.48.32: When the mighty Kumbhakarṇa, deep in sleep, did not awaken even at those loud cries, then all those hosts of Rākṣasas seized bhuśuṇḍīs, pestles and maces.
t.6.48.31: Hearing the clamor of conches, kettledrums and drums, mingled with the slapping of arms, the shouts and the lion-like roars, the birds fled in all directions, crowding the sky, and suddenly fell down.
t.6.48.33: Then the towering rākṣasas struck Kumbhakarṇa, who lay blissfully asleep on the ground, with mountain peaks, pestles, maces, trees, palms, mallets and fists.
t.6.48.34: Because of the wind of that demon Kumbhakarṇa's breathing, the rākṣasas, though mighty, were unable to stand before him.
t.6.48.35: Then, in front of him, rākṣasas of terrible prowess, ten thousand of them, all at once loudly sounded mṛdaṅgas and paṇavas, bherī drums, and likewise whole sets of conches and pot-drums.
t.6.48.36: They tried to wake him, who looked like a heap of dark collyrium, striking him and roaring, but he did not wake at all.
t.6.48.37: And when they were unable to awaken him then, they thereupon undertook a still greater and more dreadful effort.
t.6.48.38: They struck the horses, camels, donkeys and elephants with sticks, whips and goads, and with all their might they sounded kettledrums, conches and mṛdaṅga drums.
t.6.48.40: With that great sound all of Laṅkā, together with its mountains and forests, was filled, yet even so he did not wake at all.
t.6.48.39: And they struck his limbs with great wooden beams, with mallets and with pestles, raised aloft with all their might.
t.6.48.41: Then a thousand kettledrums were beaten all at once on every side, with drumsticks of burnished gold that never ceased.
t.6.48.42: When, even so, the one sunk in deep sleep did not awaken at all, having fallen under the power of the curse, the night-rangers then grew angry.
t.6.48.44: Some beat drums, others raised a great din, some tore at his hair, and others bit his two ears; yet Kumbhakarṇa, fallen under the sway of a mighty sleep, did not stir.
t.6.48.43: Others, all of them filled with great wrath and of terrible prowess, exerted their might, intent on awakening that rākṣasa.
t.6.48.45: Other mighty ones, holding hammers and mallets in their hands, brought those hammers and mallets crashing down upon his head, his chest and his limbs.
t.6.48.46: Though he was struck on every side with śataghnīs fastened by bonds of rope, the huge-bodied rākṣasa did not awaken.
t.6.48.47: A thousand elephants were made to run over his body; then Kumbhakarṇa, awakened, perceived the intense touch.
t.6.48.48: Paying no heed to those mighty blows from the mountain peaks and trees being hurled down upon him, he, his sleep at an end and tormented by the fear of hunger, suddenly sprang up, yawning.
t.6.48.50: As he yawned again and again, his mouth, like the netherworld Pātāla, appeared like the sun risen upon the summit of Mount Meru's peak.
t.6.48.49: Flinging out his two arms, which resembled the coils of serpents and the peaks of mountains and had the strength of mountain summits, and opening wide his mouth, which looked like Vaḍavāmukha, that night-roamer yawned hideously.
t.6.48.51: Yawning, the exceedingly mighty night-roamer awoke, and his breath came forth like a wind blowing from a mountain.
t.6.48.52: The form of that Kumbhakarṇa, as he rose up, shone like that of a raining cloud accompanied by cranes at the end of the hot season.
t.6.48.53: His two great eyes, like blazing fire and bright as lightning, were seen like two great planets ablaze.
t.6.48.54: Hungry, he ate the meat; thirsty, he drank the blood. Then the enemy of Śakra drank a pot of fat and the wine as well.
t.6.48.55: Then, knowing that he was satisfied, the night-rangers sprang up, and bowing to him with their heads, they surrounded him on all sides.
t.6.48.56: That bull among the Nairṛtas comforted all the Nairṛtas, and, astonished at having been awakened, he spoke these words to the Rākṣasas.
t.6.48.57: For what purpose have I been struck and awakened by you? I trust all is well with the king, and that there is no danger of any kind here?
t.6.48.58: Or surely some great danger has arisen from others, and it is for that very reason that I have been hastily awakened by you.
t.6.48.59: Today I shall uproot the fear of the king of the Rākṣasas; I shall bring down even great Indra, and likewise I shall extinguish Fire.
t.6.48.61: To Kumbhakarṇa, the tamer of foes, who was speaking thus in agitation, Yūpākṣa, the king's minister, spoke with joined palms.
t.6.48.60: For no one would so forcefully rouse me from sleep for a trifling cause. Therefore tell me truly the reason for my awakening.
t.6.48.62: Never has any fear caused by the gods come upon us, nor indeed is there such fear from the Daityas and Dānavas as this fear, O king, arising from a human, which has now confronted us.
t.6.48.63: This Laṅkā is surrounded by monkeys the size of mountains; from Rāma, tormented by the abduction of Sītā, a tumultuous terror has come upon us.
t.6.48.64: Formerly this great city was burned by a single monkey, and Prince Akṣa was slain together with his retinue and his elephants.
t.6.48.65: Even the lord of the rākṣasas himself, Paulastya, the thorn of the gods, is as good as dead, for these have been loosed in battle by Rāma, whose splendor is like the sun's.
t.6.48.67: Having heard Yūpākṣa's words about his brother's defeat in battle, Kumbhakarṇa, his eyes rolling wide, spoke these words to Yūpākṣa.
t.6.48.66: What neither the gods, nor the Daityas, nor the Dānavas ever did to the king, Rāma has done here: he has spared him and set him free from the peril of his life.
t.6.48.68: O Yūpākṣa, this very day I shall slay in battle the entire army of monkeys, together with Lakṣmaṇa, and Rāghava too, and only afterwards shall I see Rāvaṇa.
t.6.48.69: I shall satisfy the Rākṣasas with the flesh and blood of the monkeys, and I myself shall drink the blood of Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa.
t.6.48.70: Having heard those words of him who was speaking, words full of arrogance and with their fault swollen by rage, Mahodara, chief among the Nairṛta warriors, with joined palms spoke these words.
t.6.48.71: Having heard the words of Rāvaṇa and weighed their merits and faults, you will afterwards still conquer your enemies in battle, O mighty-armed one.
t.6.48.72: Having heard the words of Mahodara, the mighty Kumbhakarṇa of great splendour, surrounded by rākṣasas, set forth.
t.6.48.73: Having roused him, the fearsome-eyed one, terrible in form and might, the Rākṣasas went in haste to the dwelling of Daśagrīva.
t.6.48.74: Then all the night-rangers went to Daśagrīva, who was seated on his supreme throne, and with palms joined in reverence they spoke to him.
t.6.48.75: O bull among rākṣasas, your brother Kumbhakarṇa has been awakened. How is he to proceed: should he march forth straight from there, or will you see him once he has come here?
t.6.48.76: But Rāvaṇa, delighted, said to the rākṣasas who were present: "I wish to see him here, honored in accordance with propriety."
t.6.48.77: Saying "So be it," all those rākṣasas, urged on by Rāvaṇa, came back again and spoke these words to Kumbhakarṇa.
t.6.48.78: The king, the foremost of all rākṣasas, longs to see you. Set your mind on going, and gladden your brother.
t.6.48.79: But the invincible Kumbhakarṇa, of mighty valour, having understood his brother's command, said "So be it" and sprang up from his bed.
t.6.48.80: Having washed his face, he bathed and adorned himself splendidly; then, delighted and thirsty, he called in haste for a drink that stirs up strength.
t.6.48.81: Then those rākṣasas, hastening at Rāvaṇa's command, quickly had wine and various kinds of food brought to him.
t.6.48.82: Having drunk a thousand pots, he set about to go.
t.6.48.84: Going to his brother's palace, accompanied by a host of rākṣasas, that Kumbhakarṇa made the earth tremble with his footsteps.
t.6.48.83: Somewhat roused and intoxicated, endowed with energy and strength, Kumbhakarṇa shone with delight, like Yama, the Ender at the time of universal destruction.
t.6.48.85: Illuminating the royal highway with his body, as the thousand-rayed sun illumines the earth with its beams, he went there surrounded by a garland of folded hands, like Śatakratu going to the abode of Svayambhū.
t.6.48.86: Some went to Rāma, the giver of refuge, for refuge; some, distressed, fell down; some, distressed, fled in all directions; and some, stricken with fear, lay upon the ground.
t.6.48.87: Seeing him, crowned and like a mountain peak, grown huge and wondrous, seeming to touch the sun with his own splendor, the forest-dwellers, stricken with fear, fled in all directions.
